**Prologue**

"Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and reverence, the more often and more steadily one reflects on them: the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me."
— Immanuel Kant

When Xu Le looked up from that line of text and saw, for the first time, the stars scattered like sesame seeds against the dark canvas beyond the dust, he wasn't filled with awe. He was pissed.

*If the sky outside the Sector is this blinding,* he thought, *how the hell is anyone supposed to live with it? Staring at that glare day in and day out, you'd end up like those stray cats on the mining tracks — frozen stupid by the headlights.*

And so Xu Le abandoned his dream of becoming a高贵 female warship commander's adjutant. Under the unrelenting pull of gravity — and circumstance — he began to fall. And fall. And fall.

He fell into the role of a poor outsider working the front gate. He fell into being a man selling his body to get by. He fell into the drudgery of a male nanny, handling all the tedious chores.

And in that vast, turbulent era, he simply showed his white teeth, squinted with a dumb grin, and — wrapped in some inexplicable radiance — took one step after another toward a destination nobody knew.

...

...

Xu Le, citizen of the Donglin Sector, left behind a desolate, half-abandoned colony planet. His mind carried strange, fragmented knowledge — things no one in this world had ever learned. His body held a power no one in this world had ever touched.

He wasn't confused. He wasn't ambitious. He simply stumbled, content in his own absurd way, into the most boring and most fascinating world imaginable.

The life of an interstellar guest? It was bound to be one hell of a ride.

—

**About the Author**

Mao Ni (formerly went by Beiyang Mouse, backup pen name Le Jun — there's always a Tom & Jerry lurking in the names). Born in the '70s, stuck in Yiling, Hubei for thirty years. Active by night, lurking by day. Likes walking alone. Does not like living alone.

Once studied at Sichuan University. Got kicked out for being lazy. Went back to his hometown, got some grunt job, touched a computer for the first time, and discovered he had a talent for typing — meaning he could type really, really fast.

Got online because he was bored. Joined forums because he could type fast. Started telling stories because he talked too much online. Made the stories super sappy because he had no girlfriend at the time and wanted to impress literary-minded young women. The literary-minded young women weren't impressed.

So all he had left were the words.

Major works: *Ten Years of Yingxiu*, *The Vermilion Bird Chronicle*, *Joy of Life*, *Interstellar Guest*.

**Volume One: The Unyielding Stone of Donglin**

*A man should have the spine of a cliff that weathers every storm. He should have a heart as vast as the ocean. I may never reach that ideal — but my soul yearns toward it.*



**3: Behind the Hundred Black Silhouettes**

Where there are people, there isn't always a criminal underworld — but there's always a settlement. That's what a city is. The biggest city in Donglin District was Hexi Prefecture's capital. In those streets, aside from the ever-present drunks, the most common faces were small-time black-market traders, shadowy figures watching the patrol cops with wary eyes, and... orphans.

Donglin had once been the richest, most developed mining planet in the Federation. No matter what kind of civilization you're talking about, the people who work the mines always carry the most risk. Sure, the invention of automatic crystal ore borers and blanket computer oversight had made the industry much safer. But the shifting veins deep inside the planet — the geological changes that no calculation could ever predict — had still claimed thousands of miners' lives over the millennia. And their children? Those kids became the outcasts roaming Donglin's city streets.

No father, no mother. No father but a mother. Different circumstances shaped these orphans into different kinds of people. The Federation government covered their living expenses and school fees in full, but they couldn't stop the kids from skipping class every single day. Too young to drink legally — and with their implant chips monitoring their every move — they couldn't drown their days in booze like the old miners did. They couldn't work the black market either. Sure, the government rationed their food. But living like pigs in a pen, with no light at the end of the tunnel? That wasn't enough to burn off all that teenage adrenaline. So came the violence. The tough-guy posturing. The turf wars. Everything that followed...

The "little bastards" Deputy Director Bao had snarled about? These were the kids he meant. The ones that gave the Prefect's office and the police system endless headaches.

They had a long way to go before evolving into a real gang. Their copycat brutality didn't have much real killing power yet. But being an orphan was a sensitive label — hard to deal with. Especially since most of these kids were orphaned by the last big mining disaster, ten years ago. And the impact that disaster had on Donglin District...

...
...

"We want to see Jian Shuier!"

"Jian Shuier!"

Sirens blared. The Hexi Second Precinct — responsible for Belltower Street's治安 — had received an enraged order from the Deputy Director. Move in, full speed. Contain the hundred-plus orphans in the middle of the street.

But faced with cops wielding batons and shields, the black-clad teenage orphans of Belltower Street showed no fear. The shouting kept going — though the slogans scrawled on ragged oilcloth banners were starting to droop. Maybe the kids were getting tired?

The youngest orphan had given up on the full chant entirely. He just kept repeating "Jian Shuier, Jian Shuier, Jian Shuier" under his breath, like the name had some kind of magic to it. Though his voice was pretty much dead at this point...

"Put some damn spirit into it!" The orphan leader's eyes flashed as he grabbed the kid by the ear. Now that the cops had surrounded Belltower Street, even he was starting to feel a chill of fear. But... Xu Le said there'd be reporters here today. Said that bastard Bao wouldn't dare do anything with cameras around. So he wouldn't, right? When had Xu Le ever been wrong? Just thinking that name straightened the orphan leader's spine. He puffed his chest out, twisted his face into an even more indignant expression, and screamed at the camera lens behind the police line: "We want to watch Channel 23!"

A hundred petitioning teenagers, united in outrage, standing up to the Federation government in the streets — all for the right to watch TV. What an absurd scene.

...
...

But Bao Longtao didn't see this as a joke. He didn't see it as absurd at all. Because the moment he heard "Channel 23" and "Jian Shuier," he knew these wild kids meant business today.

He'd known this day was coming ever since the Prefect's office caved to the threats — both tearful and underhanded — from the Hexi TV station's board of directors. And sure enough, after the Prefect's order came down to the police — citing telecommunications security regulations as a flimsy excuse to cut Channel 23's signal across the entire Hexi Prefecture — the government had already received over a thousand complaint letters.

The content of those letters? Same as what the orphans were demanding today. They all wanted Channel 23 back. They wanted to watch the drama that had only been airing for two months in the Capital Star Sector. But more than anything... they wanted to see Jian Shuier.

Bao Longtao had watched that show — *Full Metal Frenzy*. He knew exactly how that girl playing the starship commander could tug at a person's heartstrings. That delicate, doll-like face. Those soft purple locks — sometimes a little messy, sometimes perfectly smooth. That petite frame stuffed into a standard-issue military uniform, looking equal parts adorable and fierce. The way she'd squint and tilt her head with that childlike innocence... She reminded him so much of his own daughter. Except cuter.

A shiver ran down his spine. Bao Longtao snapped out of his daze and noticed the female reporter beside him was yammering away at the camera. The lens had moved past her shoulder, now locked on the furious orphans. A smirk of barely concealed glee flickered in the reporter's eyes.

Was the rift between the news department and the production department really this bad? Bao Longtao sighed inwardly. The bigwigs at Hexi TV had pulled every string, used the flimsiest excuse imaginable, to temporarily shut down Channel 23's broadcast — all to protect their own station's ratings. And now the news division — technically under the same broadcaster but reporting directly to the Regional Committee — was trying to stab them in the back.

These people weren't from Donglin. They couldn't understand what television meant out here. What Federal Channel 23 meant. Just like Bao Longtao's earlier venomous comment: for a numbed populace, soap operas were all it took. The residents of Donglin — a world slowly dying, growing colder by the year — had long accepted their boring, monotonous lives. But that didn't mean they'd give up the freedom to chase beauty and fantasy through their TV screens. That freedom was the salt and oil of their lives. Indispensable.

Jian Shuier... The corner of Deputy Director Bao's usually cold lips twitched into a warm smile. Even the orphan scum in the middle of the street didn't seem so hateful anymore. But the smile froze a second later.

These little bastards had made him lose face today. If this scene actually made it onto the news — with the feud between the news and production departments blowing up all the way to the Prefect's office, maybe even the Committee — would he be the scapegoat?

Bao Longtao's eyes narrowed. He let his gaze drift slowly across the faces of these fired-up, slogan-chanting orphans, searching for... something. How did these kids know he'd be bringing reporters on a tour today? Why did they pick this exact moment to cause a scene? Was it really just about Jian Shuier? Sure, Jian Shuier might as well be a fairy from some distant star system to these gutter rats. But was that really enough to give them this kind of guts?

Interesting. It felt like someone was pulling the strings behind the scenes. And if there really was someone behind these orphans... could that person have predicted the power struggle between the news and production departments? Could he have known for sure that today's chaos on Belltower Street would make the broadcast?

Bao Longtao went on high alert. His eyes landed on the orphan leader's flushed face. He knew this sixteen-year-old wild child — went by Wei-ge, a real tough customer. But even Wei-ge wouldn't dare act this cocky right in front of him.

Then something clicked. Bao Longtao followed Wei-ge's flickering, uneasy gaze — and turned his head toward a patch of shadow at the base of Belltower Street.

But there was nothing there.



**5: That Hood Can't Hide Your Face**

When fifteen-year-old Xu Le spoke those words—voice trembling, earnest yet panicked—he probably never considered the possibility that they might actually come true. An orphan from the remote Eastern Forest Region, gushing over the Federation's purple-haired little goddess on an ultra-thin screen balanced on his knee, using a bold declaration to vent the turmoil inside him. It was nothing more than adolescent hormones acting up.

Poor people had the right to dream, the courage to imagine. But the chasm between social classes wasn't something you could bridge through sheer effort. And young Xu Le, besides being broke, didn't have a single card worth playing. For all he knew, he'd never set foot on the Capital Planet in his entire life—not even as a tourist.

Xu Le wasn't good-looking. Not ugly either. Just an ordinary teenage face—a bit green, a bit awkward, completely unremarkable. No face like a god, no pale, delicate little body that would make anyone swoon. He was just... ordinary.

His most distinctive feature was his eyes. Under thick, ink-black brows, they squinted slightly, making them look small. A shame, really—those eyebrows were beautiful. Especially when he was thinking about something. Then his eyes would screw up even more, and his normally honest, straightforward gaze would take on a slightly simple, almost foolish quality.

Of course, if someone bothered to look deep enough into those pupils, past that layer of simple-mindedness, they'd find something else. Something unique to the people of the Eastern Forest Region. A rock-solid stubbornness. An unshakable certainty.

...
...

"From fifteen to fifty... every man in the Federation thinks Jian Shui'er is gorgeous. And every one of them wants to marry her."

Under the pale green tree, Li Wei patted Xu Le's thin shoulder with genuine sympathy. "Including me. I just don't have the nerve to say it out loud. You, on the other hand—shameless as always."

"I... I think so too," the little kid trailing behind Li Wei piped up. He stole a glance at Xu Le, saw that his gaze was still glued to the frozen image on the ultra-thin crystal screen—that last frame of a certain purple-haired beauty—and gathered his courage to speak.

Xu Le slowly lifted his head, looking at the kid with a grin. "Qiang, you're ten years old. What the hell do you know?"

With that, Xu Le stood up, turned around, and leaned against the trunk of the green tree. His thumb pressed a button on the side of the ultra-thin screen. A satisfying sliding sound rang out as the entire screen retracted into a slender metal cylinder.

He ran his fingers over the cylinder's smooth metal surface, a flicker of pain passing through his brows. "This is a high-end knockoff N98. At least four thousand credits on the market. You're getting a steal, Li Wei. I'm giving it to you, but if it ever needs repairs, I'm charging."

"Stop acting like a damn girl." Li Wei grabbed the cylinder-screen irritably, running a hand through his light-blond curls. "Did you see Bao Longtao's face today? A hundred of us risked our necks—you think that's not worth this crappy TV?"

Xu Le chuckled, not arguing further. He tapped Li Wei's shoulder. "Same deal as always. If I need something, I'll come find you."

Li Wei didn't answer right away. Instead, he stared at Xu Le's ordinary face for a long, long time. Finally, he couldn't help himself. "Where the hell have you been hiding during the day for the past two years? Why do you keep dodging us? I know you don't like us running the streets, afraid we'll end up in the underworld. But the school doors are always open, man. And honestly? The government's treated us pretty decent the last ten years."

Xu Le let out a helpless sigh. "We've been out of school for years. Which of us could still keep up?"

Li Wei hadn't expected to convince him anyway. He cursed under his breath. "I'm just afraid you'll turn into a damn shut-in."

Hearing this, Xu Le laughed so hard his eyes squeezed shut—like he'd just heard the funniest joke in the world. But he didn't pursue the topic. "Aren't you going to try it out?"

The ten-year-old Qiang didn't understand what the two older boys were talking about. It was a nice cylinder-screen—expensive, high-quality, and the signal under the tree was fine. What else was there to test?

But Li Wei's face turned serious. He gripped the thin metal cylinder, his thumb carefully pushing against a barely visible metal tab.

...
...

*Zzzzzt!* A strange hiss crackled under the green tree. Pale blue arcs of electricity shot out from the tip of the metal cylinder—beautiful lines of death—ionizing the air, tracing a half-meter arc around the tree, then snapping back to the tip!

The moment those blue arcs appeared, little Qiang dropped to the ground, covering his head. The reaction was instinctive—clearly, in the hard life of the streets, orphans had been tormented by weapons like this plenty of times. Even Li Wei's face went pale. He stared at Xu Le, voice trembling. "That's insane. You still call this a stun baton?"

"It looks scary, but the actual shock is less than half of a military-issue one," Xu Le said, frowning. "The real problem is how much work went into modifying it. This thing's only good for fighting street thugs. If the Second Bureau catches wind of it, we're screwed."

Li Wei clutched the cylinder to his chest, staring at Xu Le in disbelief. "I thought it'd just shoot a few sparks... You... you're a goddamn genius."

Qiang finally scrambled back to his feet, looking at Xu Le under the tree like he was an angel descended from heaven. None of them had much schooling—they were orphans, after all—but even they understood how much skill it took to turn a fancy crystal-screen TV into a weapon this powerful.

"Heh. I'm a genius." XuLe raised one of his thick, ink-black brows. But there was nothing cocky about it. If anything, it made him look even more honest and sincere.

Li Wei stared into his eyes, deadly serious now. "Xu Le, building this must have cost you a fortune. Be honest with me... Did you really go through all this trouble just to watch Jian Shui'er?"

Xu Le met his gaze, even more serious. "Of course."

Li Wei felt like punching him. In the end, he just muttered, "You're an idiot."

...
...

Watching the two figures—one big, one small—disappear into the darkness at the edge of the city, Xu Le finally relaxed. He pulled the hood of his casual jacket over his head, draping his face entirely in shadow. Only then did he descend the hill, leave the tree behind, and take a different route toward another residential district in the capital of Hexi Prefecture.

But tonight, the road home wasn't an easy one.

Just outside Roland Street, under the streetlight, someone was waiting.

"That hood can't hide your face." Bao Longtao, Deputy Director of the Second Police Bureau of Hexi Prefecture, stood in the glow of the streetlamp. His silhouette was dark, menacing. He stared down at the boy—a head and a half shorter than him—and at the hood that tried to conceal his features. "I think we've met before. Four years ago."
